issue: Must a federal court defer to Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2 and treat attempt and conspiracy offenses as 'controlled substance offenses' for career-offender purposes, even though the guideline's text does not list inchoate offenses?

sides.position: Defer to Application Note 1, which extends the controlled substance offense definition to aiding and abetting, conspiracy, and attempt. The note is binding unless it violates the Constitution or a federal statute, or is inconsistent with or a plainly erroneous reading of the guideline.
cases: United States v. Martez Smith, 989 F.3d 575 (7th Cir. 2021)

sides.position: Do not defer to Application Note 1 on this point. The note expands § 4B1.2's text, which defines controlled substance offenses in detail and excludes inchoate offenses, so attempt crimes are not controlled substance offenses.
cases: United States v. Winstead, 890 F.3d 1082 (D.C. Cir. 2018)
United States v. Havis, 927 F.3d 382 (6th Cir. 2019) (en banc) (per curiam)
United States v. Martez Smith, 989 F.3d 575 (7th Cir. 2021)

this_court: Defers to Application Note 1 and applies it as an authoritative gloss on § 4B1.2 (the excerpt is truncated, so the final holding is inferred)
quote: A split of authority exists among many of the circuits as to whether courts are to defer to Application Note 1 when applying § 4B1.2.
cite: United States v. Martez Smith, 989 F.3d 575 (7th Cir. 2021)
